cases.answer: I'd write async function fetchJson<T>(url: string): Promise<Result<T>> where type Result<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string }. The generic parameter T is given at the call site, for example fetchJson<User>('/api/user'), and it flows through to the data field of the result. The ok property is a literal true or false, so it is the discriminant of the union. Inside I await fetch in a try/catch; on a non-2xx response or a thrown error I return ok false with an error message. At the call site I check if (result.ok) and only inside that branch TypeScript lets me read result.data; in the else branch only result.error exists. There is no any anywhere: the parsed JSON is typed as T or unknown.

The result type is a union of two shapes, one with ok set to the literal true plus the data, one with ok set to the literal false plus an error string; that literal is what TypeScript discriminates on. When the caller writes fetchJson<Order[]>(...) the type argument travels into the return type, so data comes back as Order[]. The function is async, awaits the request inside try and catch, and turns network failures or bad status codes into the error variant. Because of the discriminant, data is only reachable after checking that ok is true. I avoid the any type completely and use unknown before narrowing.

Generics are really powerful in TypeScript. You make a helper that is generic and returns a result, and then TypeScript just knows all the types, so everything is type safe and clean. It's a best practice that makes the code robust, scalable and maintainable, and it's what senior engineers do.

For a browser app I'd use cookie sessions. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt or argon2, which add a per-password salt; they are never stored in plain text. The session cookie is httpOnly so scripts can't read it, secure so it only travels over HTTPS, and sameSite lax or strict. JWTs with short-lived access tokens and refresh token rotation avoid server state, but revoking them is hard until they expire, and that is the trade-off. Cookies expose you to CSRF, which sameSite and CSRF tokens handle, while tokens kept in localStorage are exposed to XSS. OAuth and OpenID Connect delegate login to an identity provider; they are not a way to store passwords.

Stored passwords go through a slow salted hash such as argon2 or bcrypt. With sessions, the browser holds a cookie flagged httpOnly, secure and sameSite. JWT access tokens expire quickly and are renewed with rotating refresh tokens, which saves a session store but makes instant revocation difficult. The main risk with cookies is cross-site request forgery, with tokens in script-readable storage it is cross-site scripting. OpenID Connect and OAuth are about handing authentication to another provider, not about storing credentials. For a normal web app I'd pick sessions.

I'd create a composite index on (customer_id, status, created_at): customer_id first because the query always filters on it with equality, status next, and created_at last so the sort can be read from the index instead of a separate sort step. If only a small share of rows have the status being queried, a partial index with WHERE status = 'open' is smaller and faster. To confirm it is used I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and check that the plan shows an Index Scan on the new index instead of a Seq Scan, and compare the actual time. The cost: every insert and update must also update the index, so writes get slower, and it takes extra storage. With many concurrent requests I would also put a connection pool such as PgBouncer in front so the database is not overwhelmed by connections.

Writes and disk space are the price of an index: each insert or update has to maintain it. Here the right index is (customer_id, status, created_at) in that order, because equality columns go first and the sort column last, so the rows come out already ordered by created_at. When the filtered status is rare, an index restricted with a WHERE clause to that status is a good alternative. EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells me whether PostgreSQL now does an index scan rather than a sequential scan. For connection load under traffic I would add connection pooling.

Both transactions read that the seat is free and both insert a booking, so the seat is sold twice. That race is not prevented by ACID alone under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, because each transaction only sees committed data and not the other's pending insert; SERIALIZABLE would detect the conflict and abort one transaction, which must then retry. Two practical fixes: lock the seat row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the transaction so the second user waits and then sees it taken, or add a unique constraint on (event_id, seat_no) so the second insert fails. An optimistic alternative is a version column: UPDATE ... WHERE version = n, and if no row changes someone else won. With row locks I always lock in the same order to avoid deadlocks, and retry when PostgreSQL reports one.

This is a classic race: two concurrent transactions each check availability, both see a free seat and both commit a booking. Atomicity and durability do not stop it; what matters is isolation, and READ COMMITTED lets it happen while SERIALIZABLE aborts one of them. In PostgreSQL I can take a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE, or let a unique constraint on the seat reject the second booking. Optimistic locking with a version number column is another option. Deadlocks can appear when locks are taken in different orders, so keep the order consistent.

User profiles are read-heavy, so cache-aside in the application cache, for example Redis: read from the cache, on a miss load from the database and store it with a TTL. The leaderboard is write-heavy, so write-behind: update the sorted set in Redis immediately and flush to the database in batches, accepting a small risk of loss; write-through is the safer option when every write must reach the database at once. The homepage is mostly static, so it goes on a CDN and in the browser cache with Cache-Control headers, with refresh-ahead to renew it before it expires. The layers are client, CDN, application cache and the database's own buffer cache. For invalidation I delete the profile key when a profile changes, use short TTLs for the leaderboard and purge the CDN on deploy, accepting a few seconds of staleness where that is fine.

Leaderboard: writes go to the cache first and are persisted asynchronously (write-behind), or synchronously with write-through if no loss is acceptable. Caches exist at the client, the CDN, the application and inside the database. Stale data is the main risk, so a profile update must invalidate its key and the CDN is purged when the homepage changes.

First, a short timeout on every call to the provider, so our threads are never stuck waiting. Then retries only for transient errors, with exponential backoff and jitter so clients do not retry in lockstep, and an idempotency key so a retried payment is not charged twice. A circuit breaker wraps the call: closed normally, open after too many failures so calls fail fast, then half-open to let a few test calls through before closing again. A bulkhead gives payment calls their own connection or worker pool so the rest of the API keeps working. Throttling or rate limiting protects us and the provider when traffic spikes. If an order was created but the payment failed, a compensating action cancels the order or releases the reserved stock. They interact: timeouts feed the breaker's failure count, and retries stop while the breaker is open.

Start by bounding every call with a timeout. Transient failures are retried, but with exponentially growing, jittered delays and an idempotency key. A circuit breaker counts failures, opens to fail fast, and after a pause goes half-open to probe recovery before closing. Payment traffic is isolated in its own pool, the bulkhead pattern, so a slow provider cannot exhaust everything. Incoming load is throttled when it spikes. And any work already done, like a reserved order, is undone with a compensating transaction when the payment finally fails.

The Dockerfile starts FROM node:22-alpine AS build, copies package.json and package-lock.json first and runs npm ci, so that layer stays cached until the dependencies change, then copies the source and runs npm run build. The runtime stage, FROM node:22-alpine again, copies only the built dist folder and production dependencies and switches to USER node so the process does not run as root. A HEALTHCHECK calls the /health endpoint. In docker-compose.yml the api service reaches the database at host db, the service name, because compose puts both on one network, and the postgres service mounts a named volume pgdata at /var/lib/postgresql/data so data survives restarts. The api depends_on db with condition service_healthy, using a pg_isready healthcheck on the database.

Two stages: one with the full toolchain that installs and compiles, and a slim final image that only gets the compiled output. Dependency manifests are copied and installed before the rest of the code, so Docker reuses that cached layer on most builds. The final image runs as the unprivileged node user and declares a health check against the API. Compose defines the api and a postgres service; the api uses db as the hostname because services talk over the compose network by name, and Postgres keeps its data in a named volume rather than inside the container.

A pod is the smallest unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage. A Deployment keeps a set number of pod replicas running and performs rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives those changing pods one stable name and IP and load-balances across them, and an Ingress routes outside HTTP traffic to services by host and path. ConfigMaps hold settings and Secrets hold credentials, injected as environment variables or files, so the same image runs in every environment. A readiness probe decides whether a pod receives traffic; a liveness probe restarts a container that is stuck. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes replicas based on CPU or custom metrics.

Containers run inside pods, the basic schedulable unit. Deployments manage how many identical pods exist and roll out new versions gradually. Because pod IPs change, a Service provides a stable address in front of them; Ingress exposes HTTP routes from outside. Configuration lives outside the image in ConfigMaps and Secrets. Liveness checks restart broken containers, readiness checks keep unready pods out of the Service. Scaling is automatic with the HPA, driven by metrics such as CPU.

Ingestion loads the documents, cleans them and splits them into chunks of a few hundred tokens with some overlap, keeping headings and source metadata. Each chunk is embedded with an embedding model and stored with its vector in a vector database such as pgvector. At question time the question is embedded, the nearest chunks are retrieved, often combined with keyword search, and a reranker reorders the top results. The best chunks go into the prompt with their source ids, and the model is told to answer only from them and cite the sources. Quality usually breaks at chunking, when an answer is split across chunks, and at retrieval, when the right chunk is not in the top results, so I measure retrieval separately. RAG is for knowledge that changes or must be cited; fine-tuning changes style or format, not facts.

Documents are parsed and cut into overlapping chunks that keep their source. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector, which is stored in a vector store. A query is embedded the same way, similar chunks are fetched and then reranked so the most relevant come first. The prompt is built from those chunks with source references, and the answer must cite them. Most failures come from bad chunk boundaries or from retrieval missing the relevant passage. Use RAG for fresh or citable knowledge; fine-tune only to shape behaviour or format.

A web page can contain hidden text such as 'ignore your instructions and ...', and because the model reads the page as part of its input it may follow that text as if it were an instruction. That can be used to exfiltrate data, for example by making the assistant put the user's private data into a link or image URL that sends it to the attacker. Defences: keep the system instructions separate and mark the page content clearly as untrusted data, never as instructions; give the assistant only least-privilege tools, so a summariser cannot send emails or open arbitrary URLs; and filter its output, for example removing links and images that point to unknown domains. Finally, test it with adversarial pages that contain injection attempts and run moderation on inputs and outputs.

The danger is that the model treats text from an untrusted page as commands. An attacker can hide instructions that make it leak data, say by encoding the conversation into a URL it renders. To defend, separate trusted instructions from the untrusted page data in the prompt, restrict tools to the minimum the task needs, and sanitise what comes out, such as stripping links to unknown hosts. Then red-team it with adversarial pages and add a moderation check.
